question: What postoperative complication of corneal crosslinking is more likely with inadequate riboﬂavin saturation in a very thin cornea?

options.B: endothelial cell damage with resultant corneal edema

explanation: The UVA light used to activate riboﬂavin in crosslinking is toxic to corneal endothelial cells. In the presence of riboﬂavin, approximately 95% of the UVA light is absorbed in the anterior 300 μm of the corneal stroma. A minimum corneal thickness of 400 μm is recommended in order to prevent corneal edema from endothelial toxicity, but thinner corneas may be thickened temporarily with application of a hypotonic riboﬂavin formulation prior to UVA treatment.

question: What refractive procedure would be preferred for restoring functional vision in a patient with keratoconus?
explanation: Intrastromal corneal ring segments have been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in reducing or eliminating myopia and astigmatism in keratoconus patients who are no longer able to achieve adequate vision with their contact lenses or spectacles. The intent of intrastromal corneal ring segment placement is to restore functional vision and defer the need for corneal transplantation. Corneal collagen crosslinking combines riboﬂavin, a naturally occurring photosensitizer, and ultraviolet A light to strengthen the biomechanical properties of the cornea. Although there may be a slight ﬂattening of the cornea, the most important eﬀect of this treatment is that it appears to stabilize the corneal curvature. The primary clinical application is as a treatment to prevent the progression of keratoconus and postrefractive ectasia. Keratoconus is generally considered a contraindication to laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) and surface ablation; weakening of the cornea, as a result of the loss of structural integrity in LASIK ﬂap creation and BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What suture is recommended for surgical repair of the limbus portion of a corneoscleral laceration?
explanation: The preferred type of suture for repair of the limbal portion of corneoscleral lacerations is 9-0 or 10-0 nylon. Nylon suture is monoﬁlament and nonabsorbable, which provides prolonged wound support with minimal induction of inﬂammation.

question: A 69-year-old woman developed varicella-zoster infection involving the nasociliary branch of the trigeminal nerve (V ), with Hutchinson sign. Three months following oral antiviral treatment for a corneal pseudodendrite, she returns with decreasing vision, redness, and a chronic dull ache involving the right eye. Given her corneal ﬂuorescein staining shown, what diagnosis is most consistent with her course?
explanation: This patient has neurotrophic ulceration. Long-term complications from severe varicella-zoster keratitis include trigeminal nerve damage and resulting neuropathy. The photography shows the classically rounded edge of the ulcer, indicating the chronicity of this condition. Calciﬁc band keratopathy is not seen in this patient, but it can occur in many long-standing forms of keratitis. Bacterial keratitis and corneal perforation are not found in this patient, but she is at risk for these complications as well. b17d-  Michel medium.

question: Following ocular injury from a plant, corneal samples should be placed in what medium to conﬁrm a likely diagnosis for the condition shown?

options.C: agar with Escherichia coli (E coli) overlay

explanation: The mechanism of injury from vegetative material, along with the clinical ﬁndings of a white, ﬂuﬀy inﬁltrate with satellite lesions, is highly suspicious for fungal keratitis. Sabouraud dextrose agar is used to culture fungal microorganisms. Blood agar and brain–heart infusion agar are other preferred media. Löwenstein-Jensen medium is used to culture mycobacteria. Nonnutrient agar with E coli overlay is used to culture Acanthamoeba. Michel medium is used for preservation of specimens to be examined by immunoﬂuorescence. 1e43- 4d59- 9be7- fd43369a2b54)  vitreous tap for culture and injection of intravitreal antibiotics A. 85%.

question: A patient who underwent previous Boston keratoprosthesis type I surgery presents with a 3-day history of pain and decreased vision (see image). The intraocular pressure (IOP) is normal to palpation and the Seidel test result is negative. Posterior segment examination demonstrates 3+ vitreous cell. What is the most appropriate management? 1f8a8c99bdab&t=634902382200000000)  Löwenstein-Jensen medium B.

options.A: vitreous tap for culture and injection of intravitreal antibiotics

explanation: In the setting of previous keratoprosthesis surgery, the presentation is concerning for endophthalmitis. The most appropriate intervention is a vitreous aspiration for bacterial and fungal cultures, with injection of intravitreal antibiotics. In many cases, pars plana vitrectomy will be required. Sterile vitritis can mimic this presentation, but it is important to exclude infectious etiology before starting high-dose steroids. Topical fortiﬁed antibiotics are insuﬃcient treatment if endophthalmitis is suspected.

question: A 35-year-old woman wearing toric soft contact lenses desires laser refractive surgery. Her topography reveals irregular astigmatism and peripheral corneal thinning inferiorly 1- 2 mm from the limbus. Her central corneal thickness is normal. Her history is remarkable for long-standing atopic disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Pellucid marginal degeneration, keratoconus, and keratoglobus are all bilateral corneal ectatic disorders with corneal thinning. In pellucid marginal degeneration, the stromal thinning is peripheral, typically seen inferiorly 1 to 2 mm from the limbus. In contrast to keratoconus, maximal corneal protrusion occurs superior to, rather than within, the area of thinning. Corneal topography maps show a typical "crab-claw" appearance corresponding to inferior steepening. The protrusion of the cornea in keratoconus is central and the apex of the cone is usually centered just below the visual axis. The area of maximal protrusion occurs in the area of maximal thinning.

question: The diagnosis of seasonal allergic conjunctivitis can be supported by ﬁnding what cell types in a conjunctival scraping?
explanation: All 3 speciﬁc types of ocular allergy: seasonal allergic conjunctivitis, vernal conjunctivitis, and atopic keratoconjunctivitis, have some element of type 1 hypersensitivity reaction caused by the interaction between an allergen and speciﬁc immunoglobulin E (IgE) antibodies on the surface of mast cells in the conjunctiva. In seasonal allergic conjunctivitis, conjunctival scrapings reveal eosinophils, a ﬁnding that is almost diagnostic of an allergic response.

question: At what level of the cornea are the deposits in the condition depicted (ﬁgure) primarily found?
explanation: Band keratopathy results from the deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite at the level of the Bowman layer. Aside from chronic inﬂammation associated with uveitis, other causes of calciﬁc band keratopathy include systemic disorders that cause hypercalcemia or elevated serum phosphorus, as well as silicone oil (particularly in an aphakic eye), exposure to mercurial vapors or preservative, and primary hereditary band keratopathy. In ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) chelation to treat band keratopathy, the epithelium must be removed before the chelating solution is applied.

question: What is the appropriate adjunctive therapy for perilimbal conjunctival melanoma with suspected corneal epithelial involvement?

options.B: absolute alcohol to the adjacent corneal epithelium and scleral base
options.C: external beam radiation focused on the corneal epithelium

explanation: Conjunctival melanoma is associated with a very high rate of local recurrence (up to 50%). In cases with perilimbal involvement and possible corneal epithelial extension, adjuvant local therapy should be strongly considered. Absolute alcohol epitheliectomy is one option to treat the epithelium selectively. Tectonic penetrating keratoplasty is unwarranted, because the disease is conﬁned the superﬁcial cornea. External beam radiation cannot be targeted to the corneal epithelium speciﬁcally and may result in signiﬁcant local complications. Observation alone is not recommended, based on the high-risk nature of these neoplasms.

question: How can the technique of specular reﬂection with a slit lamp be optimized to evaluate endothelial cell morphology?

options.A: Direct a narrow slit beam at the nasal or temporal limbus.
options.B: Use a wide diﬀuse slit-lamp beam.
options.C: Set the slit-beam arm at an angle of 60° from the viewing arm and use a short slit.

explanation: Specular reﬂection is mainly used to examine the corneal endothelium (second Purkinje light reﬂex), although it can also examine corneal epithelium and lens epithelium. Endothelial cell morphology is typically viewed under high magniﬁcation using only 1 ocular. The examiner can enhance this specular reﬂection by placing a light beam at an appropriate angle, revealing the corneal endothelium. Following are the steps for examining the corneal endothelium with specular reﬂection: Begin by setting the slit-beam arm at an angle of 60° from the viewing arm and using a short slit or 0.2-mm spot. Identify the very bright mirror image of the lightbulb’s ﬁlament and the paired epithelial and endothelial Purkinje light reﬂexes. Superimpose the corneal endothelial light reﬂex onto the ﬁlament’s mirror image, giving a bright glare. Use the joystick to move the biomicroscope slightly forward in order to focus the endothelial reﬂex. A wide diﬀuse beam is used to optimize diﬀuse illumination. A tall wide beam directed onto the limbal area is used to optimize sclerotic scatter.

question: For the patient shown, a conjunctival biopsy is most likely to show what ﬁndings?

options.A: intraepithelial plasma cell and eosinophil inﬁltration
options.B: linear immunoglobulin on the epithelial basement membrane

explanation: Mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP), formerly called ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, is a chronic cicatrizing conjunctivitis, with biopsy revealing immunoﬂuorescent staining disclosing C3, IgM, IgA, and/or IgG at the level of the basement membrane zone. Touton giant cells are multinucleated cells that can be seen in granulomatous inﬂammation. While follicles are seen in follicular conjunctivitis (associated with toxic conjunctivitis, viral conjunctivitis, and certain bacterial infections including Moraxella and Chlamydia), these do not characterize MMP. Giant papillary conjunctivitis will show both an eosinophilic and plasma cell inﬁltrate.

question: A child has asthma, eczema, chronic tearing, and red eyes. Examination shows papillae of the palpebral conjunctiva and punctate corneal erosions. The patient is already using a combination topical H-1 blocker and mast cell stabilizer, in addition to an oral antihistamine. Given the corneal involvement indicating severe disease, what topical medication should be used?
explanation: Atopic keratoconjunctivitis is a chronic ocular surface allergy-related inﬂammatory disorder. It is characterized by a history of asthma and eczema in association with ocular ﬁndings of papillae and chronic tearing. More severe ﬁndings include punctate corneal erosions, epithelial defects, and neovascularization. Topical medications include mast-cell stabilizers, H -receptor antagonists, antihistamines, vasoconstrictors, corticosteroids, or combinations of these drugs. Nonsteroidal anti-inﬂammatory drops should be used with caution: Cases of corneal perforation, though rare, have been reported. Topical corticosteroid drops, used in pulsed doses, can eﬀectively reduce severe allergic ocular symptoms. Patients must be closely monitored for adverse eﬀects, including glaucoma and cataracts. 1 BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A 35-year-old man has had recurrent episodes of pain and redness in both eyes. Given the appearance of his right cornea (see photo), what other ocular or extraocular manifestations may develop from the known genetic mutation?
explanation: The ﬁgure demonstrates refractile lines (lattice lines) in the central cornea. This ﬁnding is highly characteristic of lattice corneal dystrophy. The patient's episode of pain and redness in both eyes is suggestive of recurrent erosion syndrome, a common complication in patients with lattice dystrophy. There are several types of lattice dystrophy (types I through IV). Type II lattice dystrophy (Meretoja syndrome) is associated with a mutation in the gelsolin gene and can have other manifestations of systemic amyloidosis, including facial nerve palsy, polyneuropathies and cutis laxa. Optic nerve atrophy, uveitis, and hearing loss are not characteristics of amyloid associated with lattice corneal dystrophy.

question: What is a risk factor for epithelial basement membrane dystrophy (EBMD)?
explanation: EBMD (also known as anterior basement membrane dystrophy, map- dot-ﬁngerprint, or Cogan microcystic epithelial dystrophy) is the most common anterior corneal dystrophy. It is usually bilateral and is usually sporadic, but rare cases have been category 1 (gene is mapped, identiﬁed, and speciﬁc mutations have been described). EBMD is more common in women, and occurs more frequently after the age of 50. It is not associated with use of multiple eye drops or hyperlipidemia. Abnormal serum lipid levels are associated with Schnyder corneal dystrophy, which is a stromal corneal dystrophy.

question: By what mechanism does the application of topical N- acetylcysteine 10 solution aid in the treatment of ﬁlamentary keratopathy?

options.A: induction of apoptosis of degenerated epithelial cells
options.B: stabilization of tear ﬁlm lipid layer

explanation: Filamentary keratopathy refers to chains of degenerated epithelial cells adherent to the corneal epithelium connected by mucin chains. The primary treatment of ﬁlamentary keratopathy is improving surface lubrication and preventing corneal exposure. Topical N-acetylcysteine, which acts via disruption of disulﬁde bonds in mucin chains, may be used as adjunctive therapy in recalcitrant cases. Reduction of tear osmolality is the goal of many dry eye treatments, but is not the mechanism of N-acetylcysteine. N-acetylcysteine does not have any pro-apoptotic eﬀect on epithelial cells. Treatment of meibomian gland disease may help in the treatment of dry eye syndrome by stabilizing the lipid layer.

question: What property of adenovirus makes it resistant to routine disinfection precautions (eg, swabbing a tonometer tip with ethyl alcohol)?

options.A: absence of glycoproteins in the capsid
options.C: presence of a double-stranded DNA genome

explanation: In contrast to herpes simplex virus (HSV), human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV), and inﬂuenza virus, adenoviruses, and many other viruses responsible for infectious outbreaks, do not have a viral envelope. Viral envelopes are composed primarily of lipids and proteins, which render them more susceptible to heat, acids, and drying. Alcohol swabbing is suﬃcient to inactivate enveloped viruses. Adenoviruses, however, are surrounded only by a capsid of primarily glycoproteins, which are intrinsically more resistant to these same environmental stressors. For this reason, alcohol swabbing of a reusable tonometer tip is insuﬃcient to prevent inoculation of subsequent patients in the setting of adenoviral exposure. Diluted bleach cleaning solution or disposable tonometer tips are necessary. Both HSV and adenovirus are characterized by a double-stranded DNA genome. Acanthamoeba, not adenovirus, can prolong survival by encysting itself in a dormant form.

question: A 56-year-old patient with herpes simplex dendritic keratitis was treated with topical triﬂuridine, 9 times per day for 3 weeks. The dendrite resolved, but the patient developed marked punctate epithelial keratopathy and epithelial irregularity. The corneal stroma is clear. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Discontinue topical triﬂuridine and add vidarabine ointment.
options.B: Discontinue topical triﬂuridine and add lubricants.
options.C: Continue topical triﬂuridine and add oral prednisone.
options.D: Culture the cornea for herpes simplex virus and add topical tobramycin.

explanation: Topical triﬂuridine is toxic to the corneal epithelium and discontinuation after 10 to 14 days is generally recommended. If epithelial irregularities persist due to prolonged exposure, the treatment is to discontinue triﬂuridine and begin using topical lubricants. Adding oral prednisone will have no eﬀect on epithelial integrity. Similarly, vidarabine and tobramycin are not useful in the scenario presented. 8ce5- 4e002ab992c5)  Bowman layer.

question: A 73-year-old woman presents with decreased vision over the past 6 months. A photo of her anterior segment examination is shown. The condition is localized to what layer of the cornea?
explanation: This is an image of band keratopathy. Band keratopathy (the deposition of calcium in the cornea) can result from multiple causes, including chronic inﬂammatory ocular disease, hypercalcemia from systemic disorders such as renal failure, elevated serum phosphorus, chronic exposure to mercurial preservatives or vapors, silicone oil in the anterior chamber, and other rare causes. Band keratopathy can also be hereditary. The keratopathy begins as basophilic deposits in the Bowman layer. The band typically starts peripherally and then coalesces inwards. The band generally runs horizontally in the interpalpebral ﬁssure, but in advanced cases can involve the entire cornea. The treatment of band keratopathy involves the use of disodium ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) chelation. The corneal epithelium is removed and the chelating agent is then applied to the calcium. Agitation with a cellulose sponge may enhance calcium release from the Bowman layer. Occasionally, residual anterior stromal opaciﬁcation is present following removal of calcium, which may be amenable to additional treatment such as phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK).

question: Following unilateral chemical corneal burn with complete conjunctivalization of the cornea, what surgical option is most likely to result in improvement?
explanation: If total loss of limbal stem cells occurs unilaterally, an autograft of limbal epithelium from the fellow eye can repopulate the diseased cornea with normal corneal epithelium. The SLET technique is one in which minimal tissue is harvested from the donor eye to reduce the risk of damage to the ocular surface of the healthy eye. If total loss of limbal stem cells occurs bilaterally, options include harvesting stem cells from a living related donor (limbal stem cell allograft) or from an eye bank donor cornea (keratolimbal allograft). Cell culture (ex vivo expansion) of corneal stem cells has been shown to be an eﬀective source for corneal surface repopulation; however, this technique remains experimental and is not available in the United States. Allogeneic limbal stem cell transplantation requires systemic immunosuppression as part of the postoperative regimen and is not needed when the unaﬀected eye can serve as a donor. Keratoprosthesis can be used in cases of limbal stem cell deﬁciency, but given its risks (glaucoma, endophthalmitis), this surgery is not the BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What is the most common cause of angular blepharitis?
explanation: Moraxella lacunata is the most common cause of angular blepharitis. Moraxella lacunata angular blepharitis can also occur concurrently with Staphylococcus aureus blepharoconjunctivitis. Herpes simplex virus is a less common cause of angular blepharitis. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a cause of conjunctivitis.

question: In a patient with fungal keratitis, what ﬁnding confers the most guarded (ominous) prognosis?
explanation: Invasion of fungus into the sclera is a potentially globe-threatening complication. Scleral extension can precede intraocular infection and is particularly concerning because infected tissue may no longer be cleared by surgical grafting. Extension into the sclera or anterior chamber lowers the prognosis for globe salvage. Satellite lesions, ring inﬁltrates, and endothelial plaques can be seen in moderately severe fungal keratitis.

question: What form of scleritis is most commonly associated with increased ocular and systemic morbidity?
explanation: Scleritis is often associated with systemic disease, especially rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, seronegative spondyloarthropathies, polyarteritis nodosa, and giant cell arteritis. Infectious and metabolic causes (such as gout) should also be considered in the diﬀerential diagnosis. Necrotizing scleritis is the most destructive form of scleritis and can be associated with either ocular or systemic complications in up to 60% of aﬀected patients. It is further subdivided into necrotizing scleritis with or without inﬂammation.

question: A 30-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus presents with poor vision and pain in her left eye. Her slit-lamp examination is abnormal, as shown. Bacterial and fungal cultures of the peripheral cornea are negative. What is the likely deﬁnitive treatment?
explanation: The ﬁgure depicts a patient with peripheral ulcerative keratitis. After a negative infectious workup result, an autoimmune etiology must be considered, and a thorough workup should be conducted to look for associated systemic conditions. In this case, the patient is known to have an autoimmune condition. Noninfectious, immune-mediated peripheral ulcerative keratitis necessitates systemic therapy with corticosteroids and may require subsequent immunosuppressant BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What technique should be avoided in pterygium excision surgery?
explanation: Several options are available to repair the defect left in the conjunctiva after pterygium removal. These include free conjunctival autograft, sliding conjunctival pedicle ﬂap, and/or amniotic membrane graft. Leaving the area bare is not advised, as this increases the risk of pterygium recurrence. The rate of recurrence with bare sclera is 32% to 88%.

question: What factor has been associated with an increased risk for developing varicella-zoster reactivation?

options.D: vaccination with live herpes zoster vaccine

explanation: Shingles (zoster reactivation) represents reactivation of latent virus in people with a waning level of immunity to infection. Most patients are in their sixth to ninth decades. The majority are healthy with no predisposing factors. Shingles is more common, however, in people BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: For the ﬁnding shown, what is the most appropriate management?
explanation: The pictured ﬁnding is a subconjunctival hemorrhage. Typically, there is no antecedent trauma. Occasionally, a history of Valsalva maneuver, use of anticoagulants, or rarely, systemic disorders such as bleeding diathesis may be elicited as a potential cause. Observation and topical lubrication are the most appropriate treatment options. When there is associated elevation of the limbal conjunctiva, disruption of the normal tear ﬁlm can cause corneal dellen, which represents focal corneal thinning due to stromal dehydration. Topical steroids could be indicated for inﬂammatory conditions such as episcleritis or scleritis, but not in the setting of subconjunctival hemorrhage. Similarly, topical nonsteroidal anti-inﬂammatory medications would not be indicated in this scenario. Prophylactic antibiotics would only be warranted in the setting of a signiﬁcant conjunctival abrasion or associated corneal epithelial defect.

question: When an inheritance pattern is present in Fuchs endothelial dystrophy, what type of pattern is most common?
explanation: Fuchs endothelial dystrophy is characterized by corneal guttae and decreased endothelial cell function, which lead to decreased vision. Cases without known inheritance are common, but when an inheritance pattern is present, it is usually autosomal dominant. To manifest an autosomal recessive dystrophy, an individual must receive a genetic mutation from both parents who, although carriers of the mutation, are usually unaﬀected. Macular corneal dystrophy is an example of autosomal recessive inheritance. X-linked dominant inheritance occurs when a genetic mutation is carried on the X chromosome and manifests in both male and female carriers. Incontinentia pigmenti is an example of X-linked dominant inheritance. Mitochondrial inheritance occurs when a genetic mutation found on mitochondrial DNA is passed from mother to oﬀspring. Leber hereditary optic neuropathy is an example of mitochondrial inheritance. It is double-stranded.

question: What characteristic of adenovirus makes it diﬃcult to sterilize instruments and prevent transmission?
explanation: Viruses are small obligate intracellular parasites consisting of a single- or double-stranded RNA or DNA genome surrounded by a protective protein shell, or capsid, with or without an external lipid envelope (viruses are often referred to as enveloped or nonenveloped). The envelope contains an outer layer of glycoproteins or spike projections. The host cell-derived lipid bilayer or envelope is vulnerable to damage by ultraviolet (UV) light, detergents, alcohols, and general-use antiseptics. Characteristics of nonenveloped viruses (eg, adenovirus) include: They are relatively resistant to environmental insult. They can persist for weeks outside the human host. The use of alcohol to sterilize medical instruments is not suﬃcient to prevent transmission of infection. 818c- 312d44d2796e)  linear pattern of inﬂammatory cells on the endothelium A. 1% anteriorly displaced Schwalbe line B. 91%.

question: What structure is indicated by the arrow (ﬁgure)?

options.A: linear pattern of inﬂammatory cells on the endothelium
options.D: thinning of the corneal stroma with lipid exudation

explanation: The photograph depicts a posterior embryotoxon, which appears as a thin, gray-white, arcuate line on the inner surface of the cornea. Anatomically, it signiﬁes an anteriorly displaced Schwalbe line, which is the junction between the Descemet membrane and the trabecular meshwork. A posterior embryotoxon may occur as an isolated ﬁnding, or it may be seen in conjunction with ocular anomalies like Axenfeld- Rieger and Alagille syndromes. When the posterior embryotoxon is observed, it is important to look for other ocular abnormalities, including ﬁne peripheral iris strands to Schwalbe line (seen in the photograph), iris stromal hypoplasia, and glaucoma. Multilayered endothelial cells can be seen in posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy and in iridocorneal endothelial syndrome and can be demonstrated histologically or via confocal microscopy. Thinning of the corneal stroma with lipid exudation would be seen in Terrien marginal degeneration. A linear pattern of inﬂammatory cells on the endothelium (Khodadoust line) can be seen during episodes of corneal graft rejection.

question: What are typical skin ﬁndings seen in rosacea?

options.B: shiny, white-yellow papule with central umbilication
options.C: vesicles with ulceration, weeping, and scarring

explanation: Rosacea is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction that is more common in fair-skinned individuals aged 30-60 years. Patients have cutaneous sebaceous gland dysfunction that causes erythema, pustules, papules, and telangiectasia of the facial skin. Patients can develop a malar rash. Rhinophyma (large, bulb-shaped, red-colored nose) occurs later in the disease course. More than 50% of patients will have ocular involvement, which can include blepharitis, chalazion, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, and keratitis. The condition may be exacerbated by ultraviolet light, alcohol, and caﬀeine. Treatment options include oral tetracycline/doxycycline, oral ﬂaxseed oil and omega-3 fatty acids, and topical metronidazole to facial skin. Ocular involvement may be treated with eyelid hygiene, topical antibiotic ointments/gels, and artiﬁcial tears. Erythematous scaling lesions occur with contact dermatitis. Other manifestations may include erythema, edema, and itchy periorbital skin. This condition may occur around the eyes secondary to makeup, soaps, or eye drops.

question: What is the primary treatment for ﬁlamentary keratopathy to reduce the severity of recurrence?
explanation: Treatment of ﬁlamentary keratopathy associated with severe aqueous tear deﬁciency (ATD) can be challenging. Filaments should be debrided with a jeweler’s forceps or a cotton swab soaked with topical anesthetic. Treatment directed at enhancing the tear ﬁlm reduces the severity of recurrence. In addition to tear supplementation and punctal occlusion, acetylcysteine 10%, dispensed with an eyedrop container, can serve as a mucolytic agent and may further reduce ﬁlament formation. Topical low-dose corticosteroids, cyclosporine, and therapeutic soft contact lenses may be helpful. While therapeutic soft contact lenses may be beneﬁcial for treatment of ﬁlamentary keratitis due to other causes, bandage soft contact lenses are rarely used to reduce symptoms in patients with ATD, because they may be associated with an increased risk of infection. Patients who use them should therefore be observed carefully. Scleral contact lenses have been found to be extremely helpful in patients with advanced dry eye symptoms. Hypertonic saline (5% sodium chloride) solution is used for the treatment of recurrent corneal erosions. The drops provide lubrication and may transiently produce an osmotic gradient, drawing ﬂuid from the epithelium and theoretically promoting the adherence of epithelial cells to the underlying tissue.

question: What systemic condition is associated with superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis?
explanation: Superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis (SLK) is thought to result from mechanical trauma transmitted from the upper eyelid to the superior bulbar and tarsal conjunctiva. The condition is associated with autoimmune thyroid disease. It is typically seen in adult women (3:1 female to male), 20 to 70 years of age, with a median age of 50 years. It has also been associated with graft-vs-host disease and following blepharoplasty. Medical treatment is generally considered to be less eﬀective than surgical treatment. Staphylococcus.

question: What is the most common bacterial cause of chronic angular blepharoconjunctivitis?
explanation: Angular blepharoconjunctivitis is a chronic infection and inﬂammation of the lateral aspect of the eyelids. It is most commonly caused by Moraxella. Staphylococcus blepharitis is often present concomitantly. Streptococcus and Haemophilus are common causes of bacterial conjunctivitis, but are not typically associated with angular blepharoconjunctivitis. HIV.

question: What sexually transmitted disease should be excluded in a 35-year-old patient with multiple conjunctival papillomas?
explanation: The presence of multiple or extensive conjunctival papillomas in an adult should raise concern for possible systemic immunosuppression. HIV/AIDS should be considered if there is no obvious underlying etiology (eg, a history of solid organ transplantation, requiring immunosuppressive medication). Gonorrhea or chlamydia can present with acute or subacute purulent conjunctivitis, but would not be the cause of conjunctival papillomatosis. Syphilis is rarely implicated as a cause of granulomatous conjunctivitis, but not conjunctival papillomas.

question: A 65-year-old patient is complaining of constant foreign body sensation, tearing, and discomfort that has not been relieved by topical medication. Given the patient's appearance shown, what in-oﬃce procedure can be performed to treat this condition?
explanation: The patient is symptomatic from conjunctivochalasis. This is a process where aging and chronic inﬂammation lead to poor adherence of the bulbar conjunctiva to the underlying tissue. If medical treatments such as lubricants, anti-inﬂammatory agents, antihistamines, or nocturnal patching are not eﬀective in controlling symptoms, surgical treatments can be performed, including conjunctival cauterization, conjunctival ﬁxation, resection, or amniotic grafting. Conjunctival cauterization has the advantage of being able to be performed in the oﬃce. Silver nitrate is a treatment administered at birth to prevent neonatal conjunctivitis, and it can also be used to treat superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis. Bandage contact lenses are used in a variety of clinical scenarios to protect the ocular surface and promote healing. Punctal plugs can be used to treat aqueous tear deﬁciency dry eye.

question: A 62-year-old woman reports chronic dry eyes. When she uses artiﬁcial tears, her symptoms are relieved for only a few minutes. What glands produce the outermost layer of the tear ﬁlm to help retard tear ﬁlm evaporation? placement of bandage contact lens C.
explanation: The meibomian glands and the sebaceous glands of Zeis secrete lipids to produce the outermost, or lipid, layer of the tear ﬁlm. The lacrimal, accessory lacrimal, Krause, and Wolfring glands all contribute to the mucoaqueous layer.

question: What technique is the most useful in evaluating for lipid-deﬁcient tear ﬁlm?
explanation: A poor lipid layer can lead to tear ﬁlm instability and increased tear evaporation. Measuring tear breakup time is a way to quantify tear ﬁlm stability. To measure tear breakup time, the practitioner instills ﬂuorescein in the patient's eyes and holds the eyelids open after a blink, counting the seconds until a dry spot appears. The appearance of a dry spot in less than 10 seconds is considered abnormal. Schirmer testing uses ﬁlter paper to measure the amount of aqueous tear production over a period of time. Rose bengal and lissamine green stain epithelial cells of the cornea and conjunctiva when a disruption occurs in the protective mucin coating. 6e53- 19c511cdf419)  rosacea.

question: A 40-year-old man complains of chronic itching and watering eyes as illustrated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient presents with several features of atopic keratoconjunctivitis (AKC), including licheniﬁcation of the skin, stringy discharge, and thickening, crusting, edema, and ptosis of the eyelids. While not pictured here, small or medium papillae (giant papillae are more often found in vernal keratoconjunctivitis than AKC) are found on the palpebral conjunctivae along with hyperemia on the bulbar and palpebral conjunctivae. Other features that may be seen in this condition include cicatrization; symblepharon and corneal changes, including punctate epitheliopathy; persistent epithelial defects; shield ulcers; and micropannus. Rosacea, on the other hand, would typically present with a malar rash and telangiectasias of facial skin and eyelid margin, papules, pustules, hypertrophic sebaceous glands, rhinophyma, and/or meibomian gland dysfunction. Seborrheic blepharitis aﬀects primarily the anterior eyelid margin, with oily or greasy eyelid crusting. These patients may have evidence of seborrhea elsewhere on the body. Psoriasis would present as red patches with silvery scales. Patches usually present on the elbows, knees, scalp, back, face, palms, and feet, but they can show up on other parts of the body.

question: An asymptomatic patient presents for a routine examination. The ophthalmologist discovers longstanding traumatic mydriasis. What is the appropriate next step?

options.A: Begin a trial of pilocarpine drops.
options.B: Begin a trial of topical corticosteroids.

explanation: Given that the patient is asymptomatic, observation is the best choice. If the patient were to develop symptoms, a trial of medical therapy would involve less risk than surgery.

question: A 30-year-old woman presents to the clinic for evaluation of ocular redness without signiﬁcant pain that began suddenly several days ago (Figure 1). After instillation of tropicamide and phenylephrine to dilate her pupils, the redness subsides. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?
explanation: Episcleritis is a transient condition that typically has a sudden onset. Unlike scleritis, which aﬀects the deeper tissues, episcleritis is usually painless, is self-limited, and is not usually associated with systemic disease.

question: What is a common side eﬀect of doxycycline?
explanation: Oral doxycycline in doses of 40 mg to 200 mg per day is generally well tolerated for external disease, mostly meibomian gland dysfunction. Adverse eﬀects of oral tetracyclines include photosensitization, gastrointestinal upset, and, in rare instances, azotemia. Long-term use may lead to oral or vaginal candidiasis in susceptible patients. The use BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What complication can be prevented if the condition shown is perceived prior to cataract surgery?
explanation: The image shows the typical appearance of epithelial basement membrane dystrophy (EBMD), also termed anterior basement membrane dystrophy. The presence of EBMD, especially when near the visual axis, can create keratometric and topographic irregularities, which reduce the accuracy of intraocular lens calculations. The surgeon may need to perform epithelial debridement in these patients prior to cataract surgery to ensure accurate measurements. EBMD has no association with any of the other listed complications (bacterial endophthalmitis, pseudophakic bullous keratopathy, posterior capsule rupture). herpes simplex virus (HSV)

question: What is the most likely diagnosis for a patient with a 1-week history of bilateral, profuse, watery discharge and the examination ﬁnding as illustrated in the attached photograph?
explanation: The most likely diagnosis is epidemic keratoconjunctivitis caused by adenovirus. The image shows a diﬀuse follicular conjunctival reaction with a pseudomembrane. Chlamydia can cause a follicular conjunctivitis, but the discharge is typically more purulent and membranes do not occur. Inﬂammatory membranes can form with gonococcal conjunctivitis, but the discharge is extremely purulent, not watery. Herpes simplex conjunctivitis is typically unilateral and does not cause inﬂammatory membranes. Mooren ulcer.

question: What corneal disease involves MHC class II antigens?
explanation: Mooren ulcer appears to be an immunologic disorder with autoimmunity to corneal antigens of unknown etiology. Precipitating factors can be idiopathic, or secondary to previous corneal insults such as trauma, chemical injury, surgery, or infection; also, hepatitis C virus, intestinal parasites, and other infections have been found in some patients, but causal association remains uncertain. A signiﬁcant number of resident cells in Mooren ulcer specimens express major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II antigens, a reﬂection of the degree of immune-mediated inﬂammation in the tissue. The other entities mentioned are not thought to be immunologic disorders. Terrien marginal degeneration is a noninﬂammatory, slowly progressive thinning of the peripheral cornea. The cause is unknown. Pellucid marginal degeneration is associated with inferior, peripheral corneal thinning in the absence of inﬂammation. Its etiology is unknown. Filamentary keratopathy is strands of degenerating epithelial cells attached to the corneal surface over a core of mucus. This occurs in aqueous tear deﬁciency.

question: For a patient with an intraocular pressure (IOP) of 18 mm Hg measured by applanation tonometry and a central corneal thickness of 490 μm, what is the most likely IOP upon entering the anterior chamber (ie, the manometric IOP)?

options.C: cannot be predicted with this information

explanation: Applanation tonometry assumes certain properties of the cornea when IOP is calculated. Measurement with the Goldmann tonometer is most accurate when the central corneal thickness (CCT) is 520 μm. Thicker corneas resist the deformation inherent in most methods of tonometry, resulting in an overestimation of IOP, while thinner corneas may give an artiﬁcially low reading. Although the exact conversion factor is not universally agreed upon (typically around 1 mm Hg of deviation for every 10 to 15 μm deviation from normal corneal thickness), the pattern has been well established. The most likely IOP upon entering the anterior chamber can be predicted with the information provided in the stem about CCT and intraocular pressure measured by applanation. The given CCT is less than 520 μm, and thus will give a falsely low reading on BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What treatment is recommended for the condition shown?
explanation: The photo depicts a pinguecula, a yellow-white conjunctival lesion that is most commonly located nasally, but may be temporal, in the interpalpebral space; it is usually adjacent to the limbus. Pingueculae do not involve the cornea but may be associated with an adjacent dellen. No treatment is generally needed in asymptomatic patients. If patients are symptomatic, artiﬁcial tears or ocular lubricants can be BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What muscle is innervated by the motor nerve ﬁbers of the lacrimal functional unit (LFU)?
explanation: The lacrimal functional unit responds to environmental, endocrinologic, and cortical inﬂuences. The aﬀerent component of the LFU is mediated through ocular surface and trigeminal nociceptors, which synapse with the eﬀerent nerves in the brainstem. The autonomic nerve ﬁbers innervate the meibomian glands, conjunctival goblet cells, and lacrimal glands. The motor nerve ﬁbers innervate the orbicularis muscle to initiate blinking. During blinking, the meibomian glands express lipid, BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A patient with keratoconus presents for evaluation of progressive visual loss. Glasses and contact lenses no longer fully correct his vision. He is interested in improving his vision but does not want to have a corneal transplant. What refractive procedure would be most appropriate for his condition?
explanation: In corneal ectasias such as keratoconus, the cornea becomes thinner and weaker. PRK and LASIK are not preferred procedures by themselves, because the ablation of tissue increases the risk for ectasia progression and attendant poor refractive and structural outcomes. Corneal relaxing incisions also are not preferred to improve refractive demands, because they weaken the cornea, and the astigmatic error, which is often irregular in keratoconus, may not be amenable to correction with relaxing incisions. Intrastromal corneal ring segments such as Intacs can be implanted in the stroma to reduce refractive demands in patients with keratoconus, acting to ﬂatten the cone and improve contact lens ﬁtting.

question: What is the most likely etiology of dry eye syndrome (DES) in the patient shown?
explanation: This patient has meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD), which causes abnormalities of the lipid layer of tear ﬁlm and increased evaporative loss of tears. Sjögren syndrome and aqueous deﬁcient DES have normal meibomian gland architecture and poor tear volume production. Ocular allergy may exacerbate DES but does not cause changes in the meibomian glands. 1 50 per pag.

question: For a patient with Thygeson superﬁcial punctate keratitis, what is the recommended initial management?
explanation: Thygeson superﬁcial punctate keratitis is characterized by multiple, slightly elevated corneal epithelial lesions with negative staining. This can be accompanied by symptoms of foreign-body sensation, photophobia, tearing, and reduced vision. These lesions usually regress rapidly with the use of mild corticosteroids but can recur after tapering. Supportive therapy with artiﬁcial tears is often adequate in mild initial cases. Topical steroids can hasten the lesions' resolution, but use of these drugs should be minimized because the lesions often recur after the steroids are tapered. Topical cyclosporine or tacrolimus ophthalmic preparations may also be eﬀective in causing regression of the lesions.

question: For the ﬁndings shown, what is the most likely causative organism?
explanation: Staphylococcal blepharitis typically appears as matted crusts surrounding individual cilia on the anterior eyelid margin (Figure 1), which are often honey-colored. This is usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus but occasionally by other staphylococcal species. Marginal corneal inﬁltrates can develop in association with staphylococcal blepharitis (Figure 2). Other possible ﬁndings associated with staphylococcal blepharoconjunctivitis include ulceration of the anterior eyelid margin, inferior punctate keratopathy, papillary reaction of the inferior tarsal conjunctiva, conjunctival hyperemia, and phlyctenulosis. Moraxella can produce a crusting and ulceration of the skin in the lateral canthal angle; this is known as angular blepharoconjunctivitis. Angular blepharoconjunctivitis is frequently associated with concomitant staphylococcal blepharoconjunctivitis. Streptococcus and Corynebacterium species are commonly isolated from the external eye but are less likely causes of blepharitis in this case.

question: Where is the deposition of copper seen in the Kayser-Fleischer ring associated with Wilson disease?
explanation: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disease that aﬀects copper metabolism. Copper gets deposited ﬁrst in the liver, then in the kidneys, and later in the brain and the cornea. The Kayser-Fleischer ring (which is not seen in all patients with Wilson disease) is characterized by posterior copper deposition at level of Descemet membrane in the peripheral cornea. question: For what corneal disorder is deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty an appropriate procedure?

options.A: keratoconus with a history of hydrops

explanation: Deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK) is appropriate in cases where the corneal abnormality is limited to the stroma, with normal Descemet membrane and endothelium. As such, granular dystrophy is the most appropriate choice. Lesions in granular corneal dystrophy involve the superﬁcial stroma and mid-stroma. congenital anomaly.

question: What is the most common cause of posterior keratoconus?

options.C: complication of laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK)

explanation: Most cases of posterior keratoconus are unilateral and sporadic. An autosomal recessive form of disease is associated with bilateral corneal changes, short stature, intellectual disability, cleft lip and palate, and vertebral anomalies. Acquired posterior keratoconus can also occur, usually following trauma. Posterior keratoconus is considered part of the anterior segment dysgenesis spectrum of developmental anomalies, resulting from abnormalities of neural crest migration and diﬀerentiation during embryonic development. The entities included in this spectrum are posterior embryotoxon, Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome, Peters anomaly, posterior keratoconus, and iridoschisis.

question: Immediate surgical treatment is indicated for what postoperative complication following penetrating keratoplasty?

options.C: wound leak with ﬂat anterior chamber

explanation: Several complications can occur after penetrating keratoplasty, some of which require medical and others surgical management. For example, with a wound leak and ﬂat chamber, early surgical intervention is often necessary. Elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), persistent epithelial defects, choroidal detachments, and suture infections are typically ﬁrst treated medically. Primary graft failure is usually watched for a few weeks prior to proceeding with a repeat corneal procedure.

question: A 26-year-old man with a history of herpes simplex dendritic keratitis presents with ocular redness, photophobia, and blurred vision. Examination reveals corneal stromal edema, keratic precipitates, and an anterior chamber reaction. The corneal epithelium is intact. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Administer prednisolone acetate drops and oral acyclovir.
options.B: Perform corneal cultures for herpes simplex and bacteria; treat with triﬂuridine drops and ﬂuoroquinolone drops.
options.D: Administer triﬂuridine drops and oral acyclovir.

explanation: Recommendations of the Herpetic Eye Disease Study (HEDS) included treating stromal herpetic disease with topical corticosteroids together with a prophylactic antiviral medication to reduce persistence or progression of stromal inﬂammation and shorten the duration of herpes simplex virus (HSV) stromal disease. Because of the absence of ocular side eﬀects, prophylactic oral acyclovir is preferred by many to triﬂuridine drops. Topically applied antivirals are not absorbed by the cornea through intact corneal epithelium. HEDS showed no additional beneﬁt when oral acyclovir was added to triﬂuridine and prednisolone in the treatment for herpetic stromal keratitis. Although bacterial superinfections are rare, in nonresponsive cases subsequent stromal cultures for Acanthamoeba may be warranted.

question: During treatment and recovery from a corneal abrasion, a patient develops a chalky white plaque covering the extent of the abrasion and obscuring the visual axis. What is the most likely medication being used?
explanation: Use of topical ﬂuoroquinolones, especially ciproﬂoxacin, can result in chalky white deposits that adhere to corneal epithelial defects. A major factor in drug deposition is pH-dependent solubility of the drug. Also, patients with dry eye using eyedrops more frequently and for a prolonged period are prone to drug precipitation. Corneal deposits are more common in the interpalpebral region because of ultraviolet radiation–induced corneal damage and because of the maximum accumulation of topical ophthalmic medications in this part of the eye. These cases can be managed conservatively, avoiding debridement; deposits resolve after discontinuation of the medication. zonular instability.

question: A 56-year-old man with decreased vision has a markedly enlarged corneal diameter and visually signiﬁcant cataract; the dilated exams are normal for both eyes. Preoperative measurements for cataract surgery show normal axial length with white-to-white measurements of 14.5 mm in both eyes. During cataract surgery, what complication is the patient at increased risk for? ciproﬂoxacin A. 57 Correct Answer neomycin-polymyxin-dexamethasone B.
explanation: Megalocornea is a condition with bilateral, nonprogressive corneal enlargement that usually shows X-linked inheritance. In this condition, the cornea is histologically normal, but its diameter is greater than 13 mm. Megalocornea is associated with zonular instability, so there are additional risks for these eyes during cataract surgery. Megalocornea is not associated with an increased risk of bleeding or malignant glaucoma. Nanophthalmic eyes are associated with an increased risk of choroidal eﬀusion during cataract surgery. Lens instability and subluxation, iridodonesis, and poor zonular integrity are also associated with megalocornea and present additional risks and challenges in the management of cataracts, particularly in terms of the selection and placement of an intraocular lens (IOL) after cataract surgery. If the lens is of normal size, an IOL can be inserted in the capsular bag. A capsular tension ring may be placed to reduce stress on the zonular ﬁbers. Standard-sized posterior chamber lenses are typically too short to be ﬁxated in the ciliary sulcus, and anterior chamber lenses are similarly problematic in the enlarged anterior chamber. If zonular support is insuﬃcient or capsular volume too great to allow stable IOL centration, an iris clip or iris-sutured lens may be the best option.

question: What slit-lamp illumination technique is the most sensitive for detecting early guttae?
explanation: Endothelial imaging can be performed using various techniques. Specular reﬂection at the slit-lamp is the most sensitive slit-lamp technique for demonstrating early guttae. Other options include specular microscopy and confocal microscopy. Direct illumination is useful for enhancing the visibility of raised lesions of the ocular surface and iris. Broad-beam illumination is optimal for visualizing eyelid lesions as well as the corneal opacities seen in dystrophies or scarring. Sclerotic scatter is a form of indirect illumination and total internal reﬂection in the cornea; decentering the isocentric light beam so that an intense beam shines on the limbus and scatters oﬀ the sclera causes a very faint glow of the cornea. Reﬂective opacities stand out against the dark ﬁeld, whereas areas of reduced light transmission in the cornea are seen as shades of gray. This technique is eﬀective in demonstrating epithelial edema, mild stromal inﬁltration, nebulae, and cornea verticillata.

question: What corneal device is shown?
explanation: The image shown is a Boston Type I keratoprosthesis (KPro; Massachusetts Eye and Ear Inﬁrmary, Boston). In general, patients with a good blink reﬂex and adequate tear function will beneﬁt from a Boston KPro Type I keratoprosthesis. A Boston Type II keratoprosthesis would have a longer cylinder captured through closed eyelids. Boston KPro Type II keratoprosthesis is more appropriate for those with signiﬁcant conjunctival scarring, dry eye, and exposure. The AlphaCor (Addition Technology, Sunnyvale, CA) is a keratoprosthesis that is implanted into intrastromal pockets. In the osteo-odonto-keratoprosthesis, the cylinder is placed through bone and covered with oral mucosa.

question: A child with short stature has the ﬁnding demonstrated in the ﬁgures. What associated organ system condition may be associated?
explanation: Nephropathy is most common in the infantile form of cystinosis (and least common in the adult-onset form). Corneal symptoms are often present by 2 years of age and manifest as photophobia. Renal damage is the major medical morbidity and can lead to kidney failure by 10 years of age. Corneal symptoms are managed with topical application of cysteamine. Oral administration of cysteamine might be beneﬁcial for posterior segment manifestations (retinopathy, optic neuropathy). excision with bare sclera B. 92% Correct Answer excision with free conjunctival autograft C. 1% excision with amniotic membrane graft D. 0% BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: For primary pterygium excision, what surgical technique has been shown to provide the lowest recurrence rate?
explanation: Pterygium excision with a free conjunctival autograft is associated with the lowest recurrence rate following pterygium surgery (0%-4%). Both rotational and primary conjunctival closure methods have performed less favorably, with recurrence rates as high as 39%. Excision with bare sclera is associated with the highest risk of recurrence (up to 88%) and is not a preferred method of treatment. Alternative methods that have been used include amniotic membrane grafting (which may be comparable to conjunctival autografting, although the current literature still tends to favor free conjunctival autografting), or excision with bare sclera and application of mitomycin C (which may increase the odds of other postoperative complications, including delayed wound healing and scleral melting or infectious scleritis). The tissue is disqualiﬁed only if the donor has biopsy-proven Creutzfeldt- Jakob disease.

question: What is the current recommendation with regard to using corneal tissue from a donor with suspected Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease?

options.C: There is no restriction on using donor tissue from patients with Creutzfeldt- Jakob disease.

explanation: Toxic medication injury of the cornea should be in the diﬀerential diagnosis of any patient with diﬀuse punctate epithelial erosions and a history of prolonged topical medication use (common oﬀending agents include anesthetics, aminoglycosides, antivirals, mitomycin, and drops preserved with benzalkonium chloride). Oﬀending medications may also cause erosive corneal epithelial defects, punctate staining of the conjunctiva, conjunctival injection with a papillary or follicular reaction, BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A 67-year-old woman has discrete round corneal inﬁltrates between 4 o'clock and 8 o'clock without overlying epithelial defect but with sectoral hyperemia of the adjacent conjunctivae. What should be looked for on examination?
explanation: The description of this patient's condition is consistent with marginal corneal inﬁltrates associated with blepharoconjunctivitis. These are believed to arise as a toxic/immune response to staphylococcal antigens that are found on the lid margin. As such, it is important to evaluate the eyelid for evidence of staphylococcal blepharitis. Poliosis, pterygium, and cicatricial conjunctivitis would not be expected to be associated with the described ﬁndings.

question: The ends of herpes zoster dendritiform lesions are typically what shape?
explanation: The dendritic epithelial keratitis common in ophthalmic zoster is actually caused by herpes zoster pseudodendrites. These pseudodendrites, as distinguished from true dendrites in herpes simplex virus epithelial keratitis, have blunt ends rather than terminal bulbs, have little epithelial ulceration, and stain poorly with ﬂuorescein and rose bengal. Additionally, pseudodendrites typically have a more raised, plaque-like appearance.

question: A 32-year-old man presents for evaluation for laser refractive surgery. His refraction is -5.50 D sphere in the right eye and -3.75 D sphere in the left. With full correction, he says his vision is still not crisp, despite measuring 20/20 Snellen acuity in both eyes. His cornea appearance on slit-lamp examination is shown below. What intervention is recommended to improve visual results in this patient?
explanation: Careful slit-lamp examination must be performed when evaluating a patient for refractive surgery, and should include a careful examination for epithelial basement membrane dystrophy. Careful attention to a supportive history of corneal erosions and/or irregular astigmatism is also indicated in the assessment for refractive surgery candidacy. Epithelial basement membrane dystrophy increases the risk of ﬂap complications during laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK). The use of a microkeratome increases such ﬂap complications compared to the use of a femtosecond laser for ﬂap creation, but both techniques increase the risk of ﬂap complications (eg, epithelial ingrowth, irregular ﬂap cuts, epithelial sloughing) compared to surface ablation. Phakic IOL placement may reduce the refractive error in this patient, but given that he already thinks that the vision is not crisp, he will still have visual symptoms after phakic IOL placement. Dacryocystorhinostomy is not indicated in this situation, and would not help the patient's vision. Patients with epithelial basement membrane dystrophy are better candidates for surface treatment—superﬁcial keratectomy or phototherapeutic keratectomy can improve the irregular astigmatism from the basement membrane dystrophy in cases of signiﬁcant irregular astigmatism—prior to consideration of refractive surgery to stabilize the epithelial layer and refractive status. In patients with minimal irregular astigmatism, but still presence of basement membrane dystrophy, photorefractive keratectomy may be attempted.

question: What is the most appropriate long- term treatment of atopic dermatitis and associated atopic keratoconjunctivitis uncontrolled by topical therapies?
explanation: Atopic dermatitis is a chronic condition in genetically susceptible individuals that usually begins in infancy or childhood and might or might not involve the external eye. It involves a type IV hypersensitivity reaction, increased immunoglobulin E hypersensitivity, increased histamine released from mast cells and basophils, and impaired cell- mediated immunity. Treatment includes identifying and minimizing allergens in the environment and in foods. Moisturizing lotions and petrolatum gels can be useful for skin hydration. Acute lesions can be controlled with a topical corticosteroid cream or ointment (eg, clobetasone butyrate 0.05%), but to avoid skin thinning and ocular complications of steroids, long-term use of such medications is strongly discouraged. Cyclosporine is the only drug approved by the US Food and Drug Administration to treat atopic dermatitis; it remains ﬁrst line and is the most appropriate treatment. Topical and oral T-cell inhibitors (eg, tacrolimus) have been found eﬀective and have fewer adverse eﬀects than corticosteroids, so they are used in patients with chronic and BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What ﬁnding would support the decision for pterygium excision?

options.B: deposition of iron at the leading edge
options.D: pterygium excision of the contralateral eye

explanation: The most widely accepted indications for pterygium excision include induced astigmatism and chronic symptomatic irritation. Induced astigmatism is most commonly with-the-rule, with relative ﬂattening occurring in the meridian of the pterygium. A history of pterygium excision in the contralateral eye may indicate a propensity for progression but is not, in and of itself, an indication for surgery.
